openers.middle-jurassic-epoch: The Middle Jurassic opens with the Toarcian heat fading into a long cool interval, from about 174 to 164 million years ago. Sea level climbed steadily from the Aalenian, and the shallow Sundance Sea spread across northwest North America, while long-isolated terranes docked on the continent's western edge. At sea, most old ichthyosaur lines vanished and new long-necked plesiosaurs appeared. On land, tetanuran theropods reached every continent and split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs, carnosaurs and the first unequivocal stegosaurs appeared, and dinosaurs left their tracks on Skye. Even familiar living things show up: the first true Ginkgo trees and the first octopuses.
openers.late-jurassic-epoch: By the Late Jurassic, the map and the menu had both changed. Africa separated from Antarctica around 160 million years ago, and in Asia the Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean shut in a scissor-like collision. Reefs of sponges and stony corals expanded across warm seas, teleost fishes began their great diversification, and the two living turtle lines had already parted. On land, the Morrison Formation and Tanzania's Tendaguru Beds buried some of the richest dinosaur faunas known, while the first ceratopsian, Yinlong, and the oldest known eutherian, the shrew-like Juramaia, appeared. Offshore, the Kimmeridge Clay gathered the reptiles and plankton that would one day become North Sea oil.

reviews.middle-jurassic-epoch: The Middle Jurassic was a time of branching. Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs, mammals forked into the lines leading to monotremes and therians, and lizards, snakes, salamanders and multituberculates all enter the record. Behind that radiation lay a changing planet: seas rising from the Aalenian, a cool interval with possible brief ice ages, a new Gulf of Mexico and a widening Atlantic Gateway. At sea, ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaurs and cryptoclidid plesiosaurs replaced older lines, preserved in deposits such as the Oxford Clay. By the close, the Kimmeridgian Warm Interval was bringing heat and rain, and China's Yanliao Biota was recording it all under layers of ash.

jura-083.title: Ichthyosaurs and plesiosaurs reshuffle their ranks
jura-083.text: The sea reptiles of the Middle Jurassic were not the same cast as before. Between the end of the Toarcian and the start of the Bajocian, most ichthyosaur lineages appear to have died out. Ophthalmosaurids appeared in the early Bajocian and from then on made up almost all ichthyosaurs. Plesiosaurs changed too. Microcleidids died out and rhomaleosaurids nearly so, while cryptoclidids, the dominant group of the later Jurassic, appeared in the Bajocian.

jura-079.title: The first true Ginkgo trees appear
jura-079.text: The ginkgo trees that line city streets today have relatives that look strikingly familiar in Middle Jurassic rocks. The earliest members of the genus Ginkgo, with ovule and pollen organs like the living species, appear then in the Northern Hemisphere. Their wider order, the Ginkgoales, was among the most important parts of Eurasian Jurassic floras.

jura-081.title: The first octopuses appear
jura-081.text: Soft-bodied and boneless, octopuses rarely fossilize, yet their story reaches back to the Middle Jurassic. The earliest octopuses appeared then, after splitting from the vampyromorphs sometime in the Triassic to Early Jurassic. Molecular evidence suggests the squid and octopus lineage split from the belemnoids much earlier, in the Permian. One timeline even lists the oldest known octopus fossil at about 296 million years old.

jura-085.title: The Sundance Sea floods northwestern North America
jura-085.text: Five times the sea rolled in over northwest North America. From the Middle Jurassic, the shallow Sundance Sea covered much of the region in five successive marine transgressions. Dinosaurs left tracks along its shores, as at Red Gulch in Wyoming. Late in the Jurassic it retreated for the last time, buried by the river sediments of the Morrison Formation.

jura-086.title: Long-isolated terranes dock with North America
jura-086.text: Pieces of crust that had drifted alone in Panthalassa finally reached land. In the Middle Jurassic, the Alexander and Wrangellia terranes were accreted, or welded, onto western North America. The Cache Creek Ocean probably closed at the same time, and the Stikinia terrane was also added during the Jurassic.

jura-087.title: Theropods split into allosauroids and coelurosaurs
jura-087.text: The first theropods to top 2 tonnes were the allosauroids. By the Middle Jurassic, tetanuran theropods had reached every continent and split into two great branches. One was the allosauroids, the first giant theropods; Asfaltovenator of South America may be the oldest. The other was the coelurosaurs, which first appeared at the same time. Among them were early tyrannosauroids such as Proceratosaurus, from the Bathonian of Britain.

jura-084.title: Seas rise toward a Late Jurassic high
jura-084.text: By the end of the Jurassic, the sea may have stood 140 meters above today's level. Sea level had fallen sharply in the Early Jurassic and stayed low through the Middle Jurassic. Yet it rose steadily from the Aalenian, apart from dips in the Bajocian and near the Callovian–Oxfordian boundary. It peaked, possibly at that 140-meter mark, at the Kimmeridgian–Tithonian boundary, probably because seafloor spreading sped up. The rising water deepened the seaways between continents.

jura-089.title: Carnosaurs join the ranks of predators
jura-089.text: Some predator lines come and go quickly; the carnosaurs stayed. They first appeared in the Middle Jurassic, around 174 million years ago, and hunted on through most of the Cretaceous. Their last definite family, the carcharodontosaurids, died out only about 90 million years ago.

jura-091.title: Dinosaur tracks and bones on the Isle of Skye
jura-091.text: Scotland's Isle of Skye is one of the best places to see Middle Jurassic dinosaurs. Rocks of its Trotternish peninsula, about 174–166 million years old, preserve both footprints and bones. Bones of large theropods, sauropods and thyreophorans, the armored dinosaurs, have been found there. Footprints of all three turn up at Staffin Bay, Duntulm and Brother's Point.

jura-090.title: Toarcian warmth gives way to a cool spell
jura-090.text: After the Toarcian heat, the climate swung cool, perhaps cold. The Toarcian Warm Interval ended around 174 million years ago, and the Middle Jurassic Cool Interval followed, lasting until about 164 million years ago. Brief icehouse episodes may have broken it, including a possible short-lived ice age in the late Bajocian. Europe turned noticeably more humid at the Aalenian–Bajocian boundary, then drier during the middle Bajocian. The Callovian–Oxfordian boundary, as the cool interval closed, saw especially marked global cooling, possibly even an ice age.

jura-093.title: The first unmistakable stegosaurs appear
jura-093.text: Footprints came before bones. Aalenian tracks from England called Deltapodus are the oldest probable record of stegosaurs, the plated dinosaurs. The earliest unequivocal stegosaur skeletons, such as Adratiklit, Bashanosaurus and Thyreosaurus, come from the Bajocian–Bathonian.

jura-097.title: Long-necked cryptoclidids and elasmosaurids appear
jura-097.text: Some elasmosaurids had as many as 76 neck vertebrae, more than any other known vertebrate. These plesiosaurs, which grew up to 15 m long, first appeared around 170 million years ago along with the cryptoclidids. By about 160 million years ago cryptoclidids were present: fairly short plesiosaurs with long necks and small heads.

jura-098.title: Megalosaurids appear in Europe
jura-098.text: The oldest radiation of tetanuran theropods began in Europe. Megalosaurids first appeared there during the Bajocian, around 170 million years ago. By the late Middle Jurassic, megalosaurines were already among the largest land predators.

jura-099.title: Salamanders and newts emerge
jura-099.text: Around 170 million years ago, the first salamanders and newts appeared. Early crown-group salamanders, members of the living group, such as Chunerpeton and Pangerpeton are known from China's Middle–Late Jurassic Yanliao Biota. By the end of the Jurassic, salamanders had reached North America, as Iridotriton from the Morrison Formation shows.

jura-096.title: The young Atlantic becomes a seaway
jura-096.text: A narrow strip of water now separated Europe from North America. As Pangaea broke up between about 170 and 150 million years ago, the young Atlantic Ocean began to form a seaway, the 'Atlantic Gateway'. By the Late Jurassic the still-narrow Atlantic had just separated the two continents. A rift spread from the Central Atlantic along the margin of northwestern France toward Aquitaine. In the Oxfordian, deep basins formed as an extension of the Central Atlantic rift; they would later hold the Paratethys.

jura-102.title: A weak magnetic field leaves faint seafloor stripes
jura-102.text: The ocean floor records Earth's magnetic field in stripes, but Jurassic stripes are faint. From about 170 to 130 million years ago, the field was weak, so the deep seafloor of that age carries weak magnetic anomalies. Found off eastern North America, northwest Africa and in the western Pacific, they were once read as a 'Jurassic Quiet Zone' without reversals. Rocks on land, however, record reversals. The oldest seafloor surviving today dates to about 170 million years ago.

jura-100.title: Iberia slides away from Europe
jura-100.text: Spain and Portugal took a long sideways journey. From 170 to 120 million years ago, Iberia slid more than 200 km past Europe as it rifted away from the Grand Banks. In the Late Jurassic, the Iberian microcontinent broke from the European plate, and the Valais Ocean opened between them.

jura-103.title: The Obolon' impact strikes Ukraine
jura-103.text: Beneath Poltava Oblast in Ukraine lies a buried scar about 20 km across. The Obolon' crater is a confirmed impact structure. One estimate puts its age at 169 ± 7 million years, in the Middle Jurassic.

jura-106.title: Lizards and snakes enter the fossil record
jura-106.text:
Snakes probably evolved from burrowing or aquatic lizards, and their earliest fossils date to between 167 and 143 million years ago. They belong to the squamates, the lizards and snakes. The oldest unambiguous squamate fossils are Bathonian, from the Northern Hemisphere, when many modern groups first appear. A timeline dates the first lizards to about 168 million years ago.

The group itself is older. Crown squamates probably originated in the Early Jurassic. Their last common ancestor is estimated at about 190 million years ago, and one timeline puts the first squamates at about 199. A claimed Late Triassic crown squamate, Cryptovaranoides, would push the origin back, but its identity has been disputed since 2023. Squamates diversified through the Jurassic and Cretaceous. By the Late Jurassic, early gecko relatives such as Eichstaettisaurus and the oldest accepted anguimorph, Dorsetisaurus, had appeared.

jura-108.title: Choristoderes, puzzling freshwater reptiles, appear
jura-108.text: Nobody is sure where choristoderes belong on the reptile family tree. These freshwater aquatic reptiles first appear in Britain's Bathonian rocks, about 168–166 million years ago, with the small, lizard-like Cteniogenys. Coeruleodraco, from China's Late Jurassic, was more advanced but still small and lizard-like. The order lasted until the Miocene.

jura-109.title: Multituberculates begin a 100-million-year run
jura-109.text: No mammaliaform order has lasted longer. Multituberculates survived and dominated for more than 100 million years, until the Oligocene, making them one of the most successful mammal orders. The earliest known, such as Hahnotherium and Kermackodon, come from Bathonian rocks of England and Russia, about 168–166 million years old. In the Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous they were abundant and widespread across Laurasia.

jura-110.title: The mammal family tree forks into modern branches
jura-110.text: Teeth from Madagascar help date the birth of modern mammals. Those fossils, with Ambondro, Amphilestes and Amphitherium, about 167 million years old, show the monotreme and therian lines had already split. That split marks the crown group, the living mammals and their common ancestor. Other sources place its origin earlier, probably late in the Early Jurassic. Mammaliaforms diversified widely in the Jurassic, and the docodont Castorocauda shows they already had fur. Most stayed under 10 kilograms but spread widely. About 150 million years ago, the chipmunk-sized Fruitafossor seems to have dug into social-insect nests, probably termites'. Cladotherians appeared around 170 million years ago, and their dryolestidans became among the most diverse mammals of Late Jurassic North America and Europe.

jura-114.title: The Turgai Sea parts Europe from Asia
jura-114.text: For land animals, Europe and Asia became separate worlds. During the Callovian, the Turgai Epicontinental Sea formed, a shallow sea spread over the continent. It stood as a marine barrier between Europe and Asia, cutting the two apart.

jura-113.title: Liopleurodon's sea: the Oxford Clay
jura-113.text: Liopleurodon hunted the sea that laid down the Oxford Clay. This marine mudstone, of Callovian–Oxfordian age, settled over much of southeast England, from Dorset to Yorkshire. Its waters also held the plesiosaur Cryptoclidus, marine crocodiles, the ichthyosaur Ophthalmosaurus, belemnites and bivalves such as Gryphaea. Its lower Peterborough Member is a fossil-rich organic mudstone. At Christian Malford, Wiltshire, it preserves exceptionally detailed coleoids, the squid-like cephalopods.

jura-115.title: The Gulf of Mexico opens
jura-115.text: The Florida Platform was once part of Africa. When the Gulf of Mexico opened, it stayed with North America and gathered carbonate, evaporite and siliciclastic sediments. The opening began in the Early Jurassic, as North America started separating from South America in a new rift beside what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. Seafloor spreading in the gulf began about 165 million years ago. As the gulf widened and North America drifted northwest, away from Pangaea, the Maya Block was carried away from the Laurentian craton. How Middle America's crustal blocks moved after 170 million years ago is still not widely agreed upon.

jura-119.title: A small crater forms at Zapadnaya, Ukraine
jura-119.text: In Zhytomyr Oblast, Ukraine, a small impact left the Zapadnaya crater. It is about 3.2 km across, a fraction the size of the great Triassic craters. It formed about 165 ± 5 million years ago, in the Middle Jurassic.

jura-117.title: Rocky Mountain building begins in western North America
jura-117.text: The Rocky Mountains have Jurassic roots. Between 165 and 155 million years ago, an exotic terrane, the Mezcalera promontory, began to be subducted, and Rocky Mountain orogenesis began. A volcanic flare-up ran in the Sierra Nevada arc from 170 to 150 million years ago. Deformation in the southern Sevier fold-and-thrust belt began around 160 million years ago.

jura-118.title: Layers of ash save China's Yanliao Biota
jura-118.text: Volcanic ash, falling again and again, preserved some of the world's best Jurassic fossils in northeastern China. The Yanliao Biota spans about 165 to 150 million years ago and includes the Tiaojishan and Haifanggou formations. Alternating tuff, compacted ash, and sediment entombed dinosaurs, mammals, salamanders, insects, lizards and plants. The Daohugou beds formed between 164 and 158 million years ago. The Tiaojishan Formation spans from 165 million years ago to between 156 and 153. The Haifanggou Formation adds fossil arthropods, amphibians, pterosaurs and mammaliaforms.

jura-122.title: The Kimmeridgian Warm Interval brings heat and rain
jura-122.text: Fossil wood says this was one of the wettest stretches of the Jurassic. The Kimmeridgian Warm Interval followed the Middle Jurassic cool spell and lasted from about 164 to 150 million years ago. Very high carbon dioxide drove high temperatures around the globe through the greenhouse effect. A widening Central Atlantic and western Indian Ocean supplied new moisture, softening seasonal swings in the Pangaean interior. Europe, though, grew steadily more arid over the Late Jurassic.

jura-123.title: The first pterodactyloid pterosaurs appear
jura-123.text: A new kind of pterosaur took to the air around 163 million years ago: the pterodactyloids. Their arrival came as the flying reptiles headed for their high point. Pterosaur diversity peaked in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous.

jura-124.title: Lhasa begins docking with Qiangtang
jura-124.text: Southern Tibet is a piece of Gondwana. The Lhasa terrane, with West Burma, rifted from northern Gondwana in the Triassic and Jurassic. About 163–145 million years ago it began colliding with the Qiangtang terrane, joining it along the Bangong suture, and the collision lasted into the early Late Cretaceous. The sutured Lhasa terrane now forms southern Tibet.

jura-135.title: The two living turtle lineages part ways
jura-135.text: Every living turtle either tucks its neck sideways or pulls it straight back. Those two groups, the side-necked Pleurodira and hidden-necked Cryptodira, had diverged by the start of the Late Jurassic. The oldest pleurodires, the Platychelyidae, and the oldest unambiguous cryptodire, Sinaspideretes from China, are Late Jurassic. The Thalassochelydia, a diverse marine turtle lineage unrelated to modern sea turtles, lived in Late Jurassic Europe and South America.

jura-134.title: Kimmeridge Clay: the mud that became North Sea oil
jura-134.text: North Sea oil began as algae and bacteria buried in Jurassic seafloor mud. The Kimmeridge Clay and its equivalents are the province's major source rock. They built up from the Late Jurassic into the earliest Cretaceous, from Dorset to Lincolnshire and the North Sea. The fossil-rich clay also holds ichthyosaurs, plesiosaurs and pliosaurs. Elsewhere, Jurassic rocks fuel other oil fields: the Sargelu and Naokelekan formations source Iraq's oil, and the Middle–Late Jurassic Arabian Intrashelf Basin holds the world's largest oil reserves.

jura-137.title: The Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean snaps shut
jura-137.text: Like the blades of a pair of scissors, two landmasses swung together. The Mongol-Okhotsk Ocean had been closing gradually from west to east since the Late Triassic. It finally shut in a rapid scissor-like collision of Siberia with the North China–Amuria and Erguna blocks, raising Siberia's Verkhoyansk–Kolyma mountain belt. Paleomagnetic data suggest its oceanic crust subducted beneath Mongolia's terranes in the Late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous.

jura-138.title: Reefs return, and crabs move in
jura-138.text: Crabs, rare until now, suddenly became abundant, and reefs explain why. Reefs had declined at the Triassic–Jurassic boundary, but in the Late Jurassic they expanded greatly, both sponge reefs and reefs of scleractinian, stony, corals. They resembled modern reefs but had more microbial carbonate and hypercalcified sponges, and weaker biological binding. Their crevices sheltered crabs from predators, and the crabs moved in.

jura-139.title: Teleost fishes begin their great radiation
jura-139.text: Today, teleosts make up over 99% of living ray-finned fish. Their major diversification began in the Late Jurassic. Early members of modern groups such as Elopomorpha, the eel line, and Osteoglossoidei appeared then. The earliest known ellimmichthyiforms, and clupeomorphs, the herring group, as a whole, come from the Late Jurassic of Peru. The oldest anatomically modern gars also appeared in the Late Jurassic.

jura-140.title: Tanzania's Tendaguru beds and the towering Giraffatitan
jura-140.text: More than a thousand bones of one stegosaur, Kentrosaurus, have come out of Tanzania's Tendaguru Beds. This Lagerstätte, known for large dinosaur bonebeds, is the richest Late Jurassic rock in Africa. It also yielded Giraffatitan, the tallest and heaviest dinosaur known from good skeletons. Its animals lived on semi-arid subtropical coastal plains that alternated with shallow seas. The fauna resembles the Morrison Formation's and stayed stable through the Late Jurassic.
